title: A Memo on 3 June, a Bankruptcy on 21 June, $3.0 Billion Gone in Three Weeks: the Borrower Refused, the Market Carried
participants: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System
Federal Reserve Bank of New York
Commercial paper issuers locked out after the default

extractionLoop.stage1_upfrontSkim: The skim was the paper itself: a market that "rose from $9 billion in 1965 to $40 billion by 1970", issued unsecured by companies with strong credit reputations and sold to investors outside the banking system — "by the late 1960s banks owned less than 20 percent", against a large majority in 1945. Penn Central, in poor condition and "unable to access long-term financing", had turned to it, and "had been a major issuer of non-financial commercial paper".
extractionLoop.stage2_structuralCompromise: Regulation Q is the named compromise, and the compromise ran the other way from usual: a rule meant to prevent "excess" competition for deposits drove the lending outside the perimeter where the rule applied — Regulation Q was "a key cause of the growth of commercial paper activity outside the commercial banking system", because "investors could circumvent these limitations by moving their funds outside of the banking system". And commercial paper is short-dated: the market's stability rests on every issuer being able to roll on the day, so one failure does not stay with one borrower.
extractionLoop.stage3_informationFog: This is the stage with the dates on it. The Fed "had tracked Penn Central's decline closely, in part because of the V-Loan episode"; the New York Fed declined to recommend the federal loan guarantee in a report to Treasury on Wednesday 17 June; Defense declined to guarantee on Friday 19 June, "leading to the disbandment of the bank consortium, the last major development before Penn Central's bankruptcy over the following weekend"; and the Board's contingency discussion of emergency lending "began before Penn Central's failure, in early June 1970", the cited item being a 3 June memorandum to Chairman Burns titled "Effects of a possible default by a major corporation on its maturing commercial paper". On the other side of the same days: "the default reportedly caught investors by surprise", the company "had retained a 'prime' credit rating", and "Goldman Sachs, the dealer of Penn Central's commercial paper, continued to sell the paper even as the company's financial state declined, which led to a Securities and Exchange Commission investigation."
extractionLoop.stage4_monopolyWindfall: The windfall went to the banking system, in the form of business the shadow market had taken from it, and the New York Fed's own contemporary account gives the size of the hole it filled: "the market reaction to its bankruptcy prevented other firms from issuing commercial paper", and "in three weeks nonbank paper fell $3.0 billion, or by almost 10 percent" to "a low point of $29.0 billion on July 15". Over the failure weekend the New York Fed's First Vice President "contacted the eight largest New York City banks to remind them that discount window loans from the Federal Reserve were available"; "Federal Reserve discount policy was temporarily liberalized to assure the availability of funds to banks and their customers"; on 23 June the Board partially suspended Regulation Q on large certificates of deposit so that investors "would switch from purchasing commercial paper to bank CDs". Banks raised "$1 billion in discount loans and $3 billion in CDs in the 3 to 4 weeks following Penn Central's default", and "Given the System's strong support, the commercial banks acted swiftly to assist creditworthy borrowers no longer able to secure adequate funds in the commercial paper market." Governor Robertson dissented: he "did not see the situations as requiring an emergency measure and judged that announcing such a change would only increase fear in the market".
extractionLoop.stage5_merseyWhitewash: There was no inquiry into the asymmetry, and the emergency power prepared for the occasion was never tested: "In the end, the crisis abated without the need for the Board to approve such loans." The market was carried back — nonbank paper "rose gradually, reaching $31.2 billion at the end of November" — while the railroad stayed bankrupt. What survived was the deregulation: "Ultimately, controls on large-sized CDs were never reinstated, in recognition that institutional investors could easily circumvent Regulation Q" — a suspension granted in one week of June 1970 that never came back.

closedLoopRatchet.inheritedFramework: Section 13(3) of the Federal Reserve Act, authorised by the Board in 1966 and 1969 for potential loans to savings institutions — "for the first time since the 1930s" — without any such loan being made. The authority existed, unused, before the crisis that nearly used it. And a corporate borrowing market built outside the banking system and outside the discount window that stands behind it.
closedLoopRatchet.newFrameworkCreated: A permanent exemption of large-denomination certificates of deposit from interest-rate ceilings, a working precedent for reading "unusual and exigent circumstances" to cover a corporate commercial-paper default — the New York Fed advised that "the inability of a creditworthy major issuer of commercial paper to pay its paper at maturity would present 'unusual and exigent circumstances'" — and a demonstrated route for central bank support into a market the central bank does not lend to directly: through the banks.
closedLoopRatchet.closedLoopRecirculation: A deposit-rate ceiling pushes credit into unregulated paper; the paper's failure forces the ceiling's suspension so banks can take the credit back; the suspension is never reversed, so the next expansion happens inside a perimeter that has been permanently widened. The market keeps the savings of being outside and gains the backstop of being inside. Burns is quoted calling the result "a vast new unregulated banking system" and regretting that "he had been fearful that the day might come when holders of commercial paper would be unwilling to renew".

decoyVsLedger.viralDecoy: That the Penn Central collapse was a surprise to everyone, or alternatively that the Federal Reserve bailed out the railroad. Both are wrong, and the first is the one worth attacking, because it is the version the people who lost money were given.
decoyVsLedger.whyDecoyFails: The surprise was real but it was not shared. The Federal Reserve had a memorandum to its Chairman dated 3 June 1970 on the "Effects of a possible default by a major corporation on its maturing commercial paper" — eighteen days before the bankruptcy. It had "tracked Penn Central's decline closely". Its New York bank declined to recommend the federal loan guarantee on 17 June, and the Defense Department killed the guarantee on 19 June, two days before the filing. In the same days the paper carried a "prime" credit rating and its dealer "continued to sell the paper even as the company's financial state declined", which the SEC investigated. That is the asymmetry, documented and dated, and it does not require anyone to have conspired: the central bank was planning for the default while the rating agency and the dealer were still representing the paper as prime. As for the bailout: no public money reached Penn Central. The guarantee was refused; the company went bankrupt and stayed bankrupt; the Section 13(3) loans were prepared and never made. What was rescued was the market the company had been borrowing in — "the market reaction to its bankruptcy prevented other firms from issuing commercial paper", $3.0 billion gone in three weeks — by measures aimed at banks rather than issuers, so that they could "assist creditworthy borrowers no longer able to secure adequate funds in the commercial paper market". The borrower was refused; the market that lent to it was not. ON SOURCING: the Federal Reserve History essay was read here; it is the Fed writing about the Fed, and it names the New York Fed Monthly Review article it draws on. That article — Schadrack and Breimyer, December 1970, on FRASER — and a Board staff paper confirming the Regulation Q suspension were fetched and verified on a parallel branch through glm-recheck --strict-sources, and are carried in at the merge with that stated in each citation; the figures $3.0 billion, $29.0 billion and $31.2 billion are theirs. The Board minutes and the Brimmer Papers cited by the essay were not opened by either session. Nobody who traded on the V-Loan refusal is named by any source, and no such claim is made.
decoyVsLedger.documentedLedger: A Federal Reserve History essay of 24 September 2026 recording: commercial paper outstanding rising from $9 billion (1965) to $40 billion (1970), with banks holding under 20 percent of it, and Regulation Q named as a key cause of the market's growth outside the banking system; Penn Central as the largest US railroad and sixth largest US corporation, unable to access long-term financing; a V-Loan guarantee under national defense authority, which the New York Fed declined to recommend in a report to Treasury on Wednesday 17 June 1970 and which the Defense Department refused on Friday 19 June, disbanding the bank consortium before the weekend bankruptcy; Board discussion of Section 13(3) beginning in early June 1970, with a 3 June memorandum to Chairman Burns on the effects of a possible major-corporation commercial-paper default; the default nonetheless catching investors by surprise, with a retained "prime" rating and a dealer that kept selling, leading to an SEC investigation; Penn Central accounting for only half a percent of outstanding commercial paper; Chrysler Acceptance holding $1.4 billion of paper against $600 million of bank lines; the New York Fed reminding the eight largest New York banks of discount window availability over the failure weekend; the Board partially suspending Regulation Q for large CDs on 23 June over Governor Robertson's dissent; $1 billion of discount loans and $3 billion of CDs raised in three to four weeks; Section 13(3) prepared but never used; and controls on large CDs never reinstated. The Federal Reserve Bank of New York Monthly Review of December 1970, as verified on a parallel branch: that in three weeks nonbank paper fell $3.0 billion, almost 10 percent; that after a low of $29.0 billion on 15 July it rose gradually to $31.2 billion at the end of November; that Federal Reserve discount policy was temporarily liberalized to assure the availability of funds to banks and their customers; and that given the System's strong support the commercial banks acted swiftly to assist creditworthy borrowers no longer able to secure adequate funds in the commercial paper market. Federal Reserve Board FEDS 2016-077, as verified on the same branch: that Penn Central had been a major issuer of non-financial commercial paper, that the market reaction to its bankruptcy prevented other firms from issuing commercial paper, and that in response the Federal Reserve suspended the Regulation Q ceiling on large time certificates of deposit of under 90 days.

citations.title: Federal Reserve History, "Penn Central Commercial Paper Crisis, 1970" (Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond / Federal Reserve System, published 24 September 2026; Jonathan Rose contributed)
citations.quoteOrFact: Read in full on the Federal Reserve System's own history site. THIS IS AN INSTITUTIONAL ESSAY, NOT A PRIMARY RECORD: it is the Fed writing about the Fed, and its force comes from the archive it cites — Board of Governors minutes of 22 June and 1, 14 and 21 July 1970, the Andrew F. Brimmer Papers, Federal Reserve Bank of New York memoranda, and the SEC's 1972 staff report, all stated to be available on FRASER. None of those underlying documents was opened for this dossier. THE SCALE: "Commercial paper outstanding rose from $9 billion in 1965 to $40 billion by 1970", against about $110 billion of commercial and industrial loans held by commercial banks; and the investor base had moved out of the banking system — banks had owned the large majority in 1945 but "by the late 1960s banks owned less than 20 percent". Regulation Q is named as "a key cause of the growth of commercial paper activity outside the commercial banking system". THE DATED SEQUENCE BEFORE THE FAILURE, which is the part that matters. Penn Central was "the largest railroad in the United States and the country's sixth largest corporation" and in poor financial condition. A government loan guarantee — a "V-Loan", "using authority from a national defense law" to ensure "transportation services for the military" — was under consideration, and "V-Loan procedure required the Fed to evaluate such loans in the Fed's capacity as the U.S. Treasury's fiscal agent". "The Federal Reserve Bank of New York sent a report to the Treasury on Wednesday, June 17 in which it declined to recommend the loan"; "The Defense Department then decided on Friday, June 19 to not guarantee the loan, leading to the disbandment of the bank consortium, the last major development before Penn Central's bankruptcy over the following weekend." And earlier still: "Discussion of the possible use of Section 13(3) began before Penn Central's failure, in early June 1970", the cited item being a memorandum to Chairman Burns dated 3 June 1970 and titled "Effects of a possible default by a major corporation on its maturing commercial paper". The essay states plainly why: "The Fed had tracked Penn Central's decline closely, in part because of the V-Loan episode." WHO DID NOT KNOW: "Despite Penn Central's deteriorating financial condition, the default reportedly caught investors by surprise." Penn Central "accounted for only half a percent of all outstanding commercial paper". Chairman Arthur Burns is quoted from the Board minutes of 22 June 1970 saying the company "had been for years a symbol to many people throughout the country of financial and industrial strength". And: "Penn Central had retained a 'prime' credit rating, and Goldman Sachs, the dealer of Penn Central's commercial paper, continued to sell the paper even as the company's financial state declined, which led to a Securities and Exchange Commission investigation." WHAT THE FED THEN DID. Over the failure weekend the New York Fed's First Vice President, William Treiber, "contacted the eight largest New York City banks to remind them that discount window loans from the Federal Reserve were available", and the Fed's signal that it would give "sympathetic consideration" to such loans "likely constituted a slight liberalization of access to the discount window, even though there were no changes to the terms of lending" — at a time when "the Fed had a longstanding policy of encouraging a 'reluctance' to borrow from the discount window". On Tuesday 23 June the Board "voted to partially suspend Regulation Q" for large-denomination certificates of deposit, on the reasoning that investors switching from commercial paper to bank CDs "would not constitute an increase in total credit flows". Governor Robertson dissented: "He did not see the situations as requiring an emergency measure and judged that announcing such a change would only increase fear in the market." Banks raised "$1 billion in discount loans and $3 billion in CDs in the 3 to 4 weeks following Penn Central's default". Section 13(3) was prepared but never used: "In the end, the crisis abated without the need for the Board to approve such loans", and the New York Fed's advice had been that "in our view, the inability of a creditworthy major issuer of commercial paper to pay its paper at maturity would present 'unusual and exigent circumstances'". THE PERMANENT PART: "Ultimately, controls on large-sized CDs were never reinstated, in recognition that institutional investors could easily circumvent Regulation Q." Burns is quoted observing that commercial paper represented "a vast new unregulated banking system" and regretting that "he had been fearful that the day might come when holders of commercial paper would be unwilling to renew". WHAT THIS DOCUMENT DOES NOT ESTABLISH: it does not say that anyone traded on the V-Loan refusal or on the Fed's contingency planning, and it names no beneficiary. The SEC investigation of the dealer is mentioned; its outcome is not, and nothing is asserted here about it.
